stem: EMI — Rating scales in old age psychiatry: A clinician wants to screen for depression in an 82-year-old woman who is deaf and uses hearing aids. Which scale is designed specifically for the older person with hearing impairment?
options: Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. BASDEC (Brief Assessment Schedule Depression Cards) was designed initially for liaison psychiatry and is particularly useful with older, hearing-impaired subjects. It consists of 21 statements written in large print on cards, which are shown to the patient one at a time. The patient answers 'true' or 'false'. It is simple, requires no auditory comprehension, and can be completed in 5-7 minutes. Reference: Adshead F et al. BASDEC: a novel screening instrument for depression in elderly medical inpatients. BMJ 1992;305(6850):397.
GDS-15 is designed for older adults and avoids somatic items but is not specifically designed for hearing-impaired subjects.
Cornell Scale is for detecting depression in people with dementia, not specifically for hearing impairment.
HAM-D has many somatic items making it less appropriate for older adults, and is not adapted for hearing impairment.
MADRS is sensitive to change but not specifically developed for older adults or hearing impairment.
PHQ-9 is a general screening tool, not designed for older adults with hearing loss.
HADS was developed for medical outpatients, not specifically for older adults.
BDI-II has somatic items and is not designed for hearing-impaired older adults.
CIS-R is a structured diagnostic interview, not a screening tool for the hearing-impaired elderly.
MMSE is a cognitive screening tool, not a depression scale.
teaching_point: BASDEC (Brief Assessment Schedule Depression Cards) was designed initially for liaison psychiatry and is particularly useful with older, hearing-impaired subjects. It consists of 21 statements written in large print on cards, which are shown to the patient one at a time. The patient answers 'true' or 'false'. It is simple, requires no auditory comprehension, and can be completed in 5-7 minutes. Reference: Adshead F et al. BASDEC: a novel screening instrument for depression in elderly medical inpatients. BMJ 1992;305(6850):397.
source: SPMM EMI Old Age; Adshead et al. BMJ 1992

stem: EMI — Rating scales in old age psychiatry: A liaison psychiatrist is asked to assess for depression in a 79-year-old nursing home resident with moderate dementia (MMSE 14/30). The patient has difficulty reporting subjective symptoms. Which scale is BEST validated for detecting depression in people with dementia using information from both the patient and an informant?
options: Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. The Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia is an interviewer-administered 19-item scale that incorporates information from both the patient AND an informant (carer or nurse). It was specifically designed and validated for assessing depression in patients with dementia. Items cover mood, physical symptoms, cyclic functions, and ideational disturbances. It has good inter-rater reliability and validity. GDS is preferred for cognitively intact older adults but cannot be used reliably once MMSE falls below 15. Reference: Alexopoulos GS et al. Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia. Biol Psychiatry 1988;23(3):271-84.
GDS, although designed for older adults, relies on self-report and is difficult to use in patients with moderate-to-severe dementia.
BASDEC is for hearing-impaired older adults but is self-report; not the best validated for dementia.
HAM-D has somatic items and is not validated for use in dementia.
MADRS is a clinician-rated scale but not validated in dementia populations as a depression-specific tool.
PHQ-9 requires self-report; unreliable in moderate dementia.
NPI assesses neuropsychiatric symptoms broadly (including depression) but is not exclusively a depression scale.
CMAI measures agitation specifically, not depression.
BEHAVE-AD assesses behavioural symptoms in Alzheimer's disease broadly.
Zung scale is self-report, not appropriate for dementia patients.
teaching_point: The Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia is an interviewer-administered 19-item scale that incorporates information from both the patient AND an informant (carer or nurse). It was specifically designed and validated for assessing depression in patients with dementia. Items cover mood, physical symptoms, cyclic functions, and ideational disturbances. It has good inter-rater reliability and validity. GDS is preferred for cognitively intact older adults but cannot be used reliably once MMSE falls below 15. Reference: Alexopoulos GS et al. Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia. Biol Psychiatry 1988;23(3):271-84.
source: SPMM EMI Old Age; Alexopoulos et al. 1988

stem: EMI — Rating scales in old age psychiatry: A clinician wants to screen for depression in a 76-year-old woman with no cognitive impairment who is being seen in a memory clinic. Which scale is MOST appropriate for older adults as it focuses on cognitive and psychological symptoms rather than somatic items?
options: Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. The Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS), originally a 30-item and now commonly a 15-item short form, was specifically designed for older adults. It avoids somatic questions, making it the best choice when physical illness might confound depression scores. A GDS-15 score of ≥ 5 suggests possible depression. It takes 4-5 minutes to administer and has good sensitivity and specificity in older populations. It relies on self-report and requires only mild cognitive function to complete reliably. Reference: Yesavage JA et al. Development and validation of a geriatric depression screening scale. J Psychiatr Res 1983;17(1):37-49.
HAM-D has a number of somatic items (insomnia, somatic symptoms, weight loss), making it less appropriate for older adults where physical comorbidity is common — may inflate scores.
Cornell scale is designed for depression in dementia, not for cognitively intact older adults.
BASDEC is for hearing-impaired older adults, not the general older population.
MADRS is sensitive and has fewer somatic items than HAM-D but is not specifically designed for older adults.
PHQ-9 includes somatic items (sleep, appetite) and is a general tool.
HADS excludes somatic items but was designed for medical outpatients, not specifically older adults.
BDI-II has somatic items and is a general adult tool.
EQ-5D is a quality-of-life measure, not a depression scale.
Zung is a self-rating scale not specifically designed to minimise somatic confounds.
teaching_point: The Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS), originally a 30-item and now commonly a 15-item short form, was specifically designed for older adults. It avoids somatic questions, making it the best choice when physical illness might confound depression scores. A GDS-15 score of ≥ 5 suggests possible depression. It takes 4-5 minutes to administer and has good sensitivity and specificity in older populations. It relies on self-report and requires only mild cognitive function to complete reliably. Reference: Yesavage JA et al. Development and validation of a geriatric depression screening scale. J Psychiatr Res 1983;17(1):37-49.
source: SPMM EMI Old Age; Yesavage et al. 1983

EMI — Antidementia drug side effects: Identify the MOST likely side effect of cholinesterase inhibitors corresponding to each description.

A predictable side effect due to excessive cholinergic stimulation:
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Insomnia is a predictable side effect of cholinesterase inhibitors due to excessive central cholinergic stimulation. This is why donepezil is often given in the morning rather than at bedtime if insomnia occurs. Other predictable cholinergic effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, bradycardia, and muscle cramps. Most side effects are dose-dependent and improve with gradual dose titration. Reference: BNF 2023; NICE TA217.
Bradycardia is a cardiovascular effect of cholinergic stimulation but is not the most predictable side effect — insomnia is more directly linked to central cholinergic activation.
Nausea is the most common GI side effect, not the 'predictable side effect due to excessive cholinergic stimulation' specifically.
Weight loss occurs with long-term treatment but is not the most predictable effect.
Diarrhoea is a common GI effect but not the described 'predictable effect'.
Muscle cramps can occur but are less predictable and less common.
Dizziness can occur due to hypotension or bradycardia, not directly due to cholinergic excess.
Urinary incontinence can occur but is not the most predictable.
Rash is rare and idiosyncratic, not predictable.
Abnormal LFTs are associated with rivastigmine and donepezil but are not the classic predictable cholinergic effect.
teaching_point: Insomnia is a predictable side effect of cholinesterase inhibitors due to excessive central cholinergic stimulation. This is why donepezil is often given in the morning rather than at bedtime if insomnia occurs. Other predictable cholinergic effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, bradycardia, and muscle cramps. Most side effects are dose-dependent and improve with gradual dose titration. Reference: BNF 2023; NICE TA217.

stem: EMI — Antidementia drug side effects: Identify the MOST common cardiovascular side effect occurring with all commonly prescribed cholinesterase inhibitors:
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Cholinesterase inhibitors have a vagotonic effect on the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, causing bradycardia. This effect is dose-dependent and is of particular concern in patients with sick sinus syndrome, other supraventricular conduction disturbances, or those taking beta-blockers or calcium-channel blockers that slow heart rate. Baseline ECG and pulse monitoring are recommended before and during titration. Reference: BNF 2023; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th ed.
Hypertension is not a known side effect of cholinesterase inhibitors.
Tachycardia is the opposite of the vagotonic (cholinergic) effect.
Atrial fibrillation is not a documented common side effect of these drugs.
Prolonged QT interval is more associated with antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol, ziprasidone), not cholinesterase inhibitors.
Postural hypotension occurs but bradycardia is more common and predictable.
Heart block is a rare severe effect in patients with pre-existing conduction disease, not the 'most common'.
Myocardial infarction is not a known side effect.
Ventricular tachycardia is not associated.
Palpitations are non-specific and may represent the sensation of bradycardia.
teaching_point: Cholinesterase inhibitors have a vagotonic effect on the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, causing bradycardia. This effect is dose-dependent and is of particular concern in patients with sick sinus syndrome, other supraventricular conduction disturbances, or those taking beta-blockers or calcium-channel blockers that slow heart rate. Baseline ECG and pulse monitoring are recommended before and during titration. Reference: BNF 2023; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th ed.
source: SPMM EMI Old Age; BNF 2023; Maudsley 14th ed

stem: EMI — Antidementia drug side effects: Identify the MOST frequent gastrointestinal side effect from the commonly prescribed cholinesterase inhibitors:
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Nausea is the most common gastrointestinal side effect reported with all three cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine), occurring in approximately 20-30% of patients during titration. Other frequent GI effects include vomiting, diarrhoea, anorexia, and abdominal pain. These side effects are dose-dependent and often improve with continued use. The key management strategy is slow dose titration and taking medication with food. Reference: BNF 2023; NICE TA217.
Vomiting is also common but nausea is more frequent and occurs in 20-30% of patients.
Diarrhoea is common but less frequent than nausea.
Constipation is not a characteristic side effect of cholinesterase inhibitors (they increase peristalsis).
Dyspepsia occurs but is less frequent than nausea.
Abdominal pain is less common than nausea.
Anorexia is common but nausea is the most frequent GI complaint.
Dysphagia is not a known cholinesterase inhibitor side effect.
GI bleeding is not associated.
Pancreatitis is extremely rare and not the most frequent.
teaching_point: Nausea is the most common gastrointestinal side effect reported with all three cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine), occurring in approximately 20-30% of patients during titration. Other frequent GI effects include vomiting, diarrhoea, anorexia, and abdominal pain. These side effects are dose-dependent and often improve with continued use. The key management strategy is slow dose titration and taking medication with food. Reference: BNF 2023; NICE TA217.

stem: EMI — Delirium: In a 75-year-old man with an acute confusional state, which of the following is the MOST important first step in management?
options: Identify and treat the underlying cause
Refer to psychiatric intensive care unit
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. NICE CG103 (2010) for delirium management emphasises: (1) identify and treat the underlying cause as the priority (infection, electrolyte imbalance, medication effect, organ failure, etc.), (2) provide reassurance and orientation (non-pharmacological), (3) involve family/carers, (4) only use short-term antipsychotics (haloperidol 0.5mg PRN, max 5mg/24h) if the patient is distressed or at risk. The 4AT is the recommended screening tool. Reference: NICE CG103 (2010).
Haloperidol should only be used if the patient is severely agitated or at risk, after non-pharmacological measures have failed and underlying causes are being addressed.
Lorazepam is not first-line (except in alcohol withdrawal or certain seizure-related deliria), as benzodiazepines can worsen confusion.
Physical restraints are to be avoided unless absolutely necessary (immediate danger to self/others) — they increase agitation and injury risk.
CT head is indicated if there are focal neurological signs, head injury history, or no identifiable cause — not the universal first step.
Empiric antibiotics are only indicated if infection is suspected based on history, examination, or investigations.
IV thiamine is indicated if Wernicke's encephalopathy is suspected (alcohol dependence), not for all delirium.
MRI brain is not indicated as a routine first step.
Rivastigmine is not recommended for delirium management and may increase harm.
PICU referral is for severe behavioural disturbance after initial assessment and management.
teaching_point: NICE CG103 (2010) for delirium management emphasises: (1) identify and treat the underlying cause as the priority (infection, electrolyte imbalance, medication effect, organ failure, etc.), (2) provide reassurance and orientation (non-pharmacological), (3) involve family/carers, (4) only use short-term antipsychotics (haloperidol 0.5mg PRN, max 5mg/24h) if the patient is distressed or at risk. The 4AT is the recommended screening tool. Reference: NICE CG103 (2010).

stem:
EMI — Neuroimaging in dementia: Identify the MOST likely finding on each neuroimaging modality in Alzheimer's disease.

CT scan:
options: Cortical atrophy, particularly parietal and temporal lobes, with third ventricular dilatation
Reduced cerebral blood flow in temporal and posterior parietal regions
Reduced glucose metabolism in temporal and posterior parietal lobes
Reduced levels of N-acetylaspartate (NAA) on spectroscopy
Frontal and anterior temporal lobe atrophy
Asymmetric atrophy of the dominant temporal lobe
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. CT scan in Alzheimer's disease classically shows cortical atrophy, most prominent in the medial temporal (including hippocampus), parietal, and temporal lobes, with associated dilatation of the third ventricle and temporal horns. The degree of atrophy correlates with cognitive impairment. In advanced disease, frontal lobe involvement is also visible. CT is less sensitive than MRI for detecting hippocampal atrophy. Reference: Scheltens P et al. Atrophy of medial temporal lobes on MRI in 'probable' Alzheimer's disease and normal ageing. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1992;55(10):967-72.
Reduced cerebral blood flow in temporal and parietal regions is seen on SPECT, not CT.
Reduced glucose metabolism in temporal and posterior parietal lobes is seen on PET, not CT.
Reduced NAA is seen on MR spectroscopy, not CT.
Multiple white matter hyperintensities are seen on MRI (T2/FLAIR), suggesting small vessel disease, not Alzheimer's.
Frontal and anterior temporal atrophy suggests frontotemporal dementia, not Alzheimer's.
Normal imaging is possible in early Alzheimer's but is not the 'most likely' finding.
Asymmetric temporal atrophy is more characteristic of semantic dementia (a form of FTD).
Hippocampal sclerosis is seen on MRI, and is associated with advanced age and TDP-43 pathology.
Cerebellar atrophy with brainstem involvement is seen in multiple system atrophy or spinocerebellar ataxia.
teaching_point: CT scan in Alzheimer's disease classically shows cortical atrophy, most prominent in the medial temporal (including hippocampus), parietal, and temporal lobes, with associated dilatation of the third ventricle and temporal horns. The degree of atrophy correlates with cognitive impairment. In advanced disease, frontal lobe involvement is also visible. CT is less sensitive than MRI for detecting hippocampal atrophy. Reference: Scheltens P et al. Atrophy of medial temporal lobes on MRI in 'probable' Alzheimer's disease and normal ageing. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1992;55(10):967-72.

stem: EMI — Neuroimaging in dementia: Identify the MOST likely SPECT finding in Alzheimer's disease:
options: Reduced cerebral blood flow in temporal and posterior parietal regions
Reduced glucose metabolism in temporoparietal cortex
Reduced levels of NAA on MR spectroscopy
Decreased dopamine transporter binding in the basal ganglia
Global reduction in cerebral blood flow
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. SPECT (Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography) measures regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF). In Alzheimer's disease, a characteristic pattern of reduced blood flow is seen in the temporal and posterior parietal regions, often bilaterally. This pattern can help distinguish Alzheimer's disease from frontotemporal dementia (which shows frontal hypoperfusion) and DLB (occipital hypoperfusion). SPECT is not routinely recommended by NICE for dementia diagnosis but can be useful in diagnostically challenging cases. Reference: NICE NG97; Dougall NJ et al. Systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of 99mTc-HMPAO-SPECT in dementia. Am J Geriatr Psychiatry 2004;12(6):554-70.
Cortical atrophy is seen on CT/MRI structural imaging, not on SPECT (which measures blood flow).
Reduced glucose metabolism is seen on PET (FDG-PET), not SPECT.
Reduced NAA on MR spectroscopy is an MRS finding.
Decreased dopamine transporter binding in basal ganglia is seen on DaTSCAN (FP-CIT SPECT) in DLB, not Alzheimer's.
Increased amyloid is detected by PET (amyloid-PET), not SPECT.
Frontal lobe hypoperfusion is seen in frontotemporal dementia.
Global blood flow reduction is non-specific and not characteristic of Alzheimer's.
Occipital hypoperfusion is characteristic of DLB.
Focal temporal hyperperfusion is not a recognised Alzheimer's finding.
teaching_point: SPECT (Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography) measures regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF). In Alzheimer's disease, a characteristic pattern of reduced blood flow is seen in the temporal and posterior parietal regions, often bilaterally. This pattern can help distinguish Alzheimer's disease from frontotemporal dementia (which shows frontal hypoperfusion) and DLB (occipital hypoperfusion). SPECT is not routinely recommended by NICE for dementia diagnosis but can be useful in diagnostically challenging cases. Reference: NICE NG97; Dougall NJ et al. Systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of 99mTc-HMPAO-SPECT in dementia. Am J Geriatr Psychiatry 2004;12(6):554-70.

stem: EMI — Neuroimaging in dementia: In Parkinson's disease dementia versus dementia with Lewy bodies, the presence of which imaging finding BEST supports DLB over PDD?
options: Both share identical underlying pathology (Lewy bodies); the distinction is temporal (1-year rule)
White matter hyperintensities in periventricular regions
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) share identical pathology — Lewy body deposition, with a-synuclein aggregates. The diagnostic distinction (the '1-year rule') is temporal: DLB is diagnosed when dementia develops before or within 1 year of the onset of parkinsonism; PDD is diagnosed when dementia develops more than 1 year after well-established Parkinson's disease. From a practical clinical standpoint, they are the same disease entity on a continuum. The 2017 McKeith consensus criteria removed this strict distinction and now define DLB as the overarching term for the Lewy body dementia spectrum. Reference: McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of DLB: Fourth consensus report. Neurology 2017;89(1):88-100.
Hippocampal atrophy is more characteristic of Alzheimer's disease.
Occipital hypoperfusion is seen in both PDD and DLB and does not differentiate them.
Frontal lobe atrophy is more characteristic of FTD.
Elevated amyloid PET signal indicates co-existent Alzheimer's pathology, which is common in both but does not differentiate them.
Parietal lobe atrophy is more Alzheimer's disease.
Cerebellar atrophy is not a feature of Lewy body spectrum disorders.
Putaminal atrophy on MRI is a feature of some rarer neurodegenerative conditions like SCA or neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation.
Thalamic MRS changes are not diagnostic in this context.
White matter hyperintensities represent small vessel disease, not specific to Lewy body pathology.
teaching_point: Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) share identical pathology — Lewy body deposition, with a-synuclein aggregates. The diagnostic distinction (the '1-year rule') is temporal: DLB is diagnosed when dementia develops before or within 1 year of the onset of parkinsonism; PDD is diagnosed when dementia develops more than 1 year after well-established Parkinson's disease. From a practical clinical standpoint, they are the same disease entity on a continuum. The 2017 McKeith consensus criteria removed this strict distinction and now define DLB as the overarching term for the Lewy body dementia spectrum. Reference: McKeith IG et al. Diagnosis and management of DLB: Fourth consensus report. Neurology 2017;89(1):88-100.

stem: EMI — Psychotherapy defence mechanisms: A 45-year-old patient with paranoid personality disorder tells his psychiatrist, 'I'm not paranoid — you're the one who can't be trusted, you probably work for the government.' Which defence mechanism is most likely being used?
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Projection is an ego defence mechanism in which an individual unconsciously attributes their own unacceptable thoughts, feelings, or impulses onto another person. It is a primitive defence commonly seen in paranoid personality disorder and paranoia in psychotic disorders. The patient cannot tolerate his own distrustfulness, so he attributes it to the psychiatrist instead. This is a classic SPMM EMI pattern. Reference: Freud S. (1896). Further remarks on the neuro-psychoses of defence. Standard Edition, Vol 3.
Denial would involve refusing to acknowledge the paranoid feelings exist at all.
Rationalisation involves creating logical excuses for behaviour.
Splitting involves seeing people as all-good or all-bad, not attributing one's own traits to others.
Displacement involves redirecting impulses to a safer target (e.g., anger at boss taken out on spouse).
Reaction formation involves behaving in the opposite way to one's true feelings.
Intellectualisation involves using abstract thinking to avoid emotional distress.
Isolation of affect involves separating an idea from its associated emotion.
Acting out involves expressing impulses through action rather than words.
Sublimation involves channeling unacceptable impulses into socially valued behaviours.
teaching_point: Projection is an ego defence mechanism in which an individual unconsciously attributes their own unacceptable thoughts, feelings, or impulses onto another person. It is a primitive defence commonly seen in paranoid personality disorder and paranoia in psychotic disorders. The patient cannot tolerate his own distrustfulness, so he attributes it to the psychiatrist instead. This is a classic SPMM EMI pattern. Reference: Freud S. (1896). Further remarks on the neuro-psychoses of defence. Standard Edition, Vol 3.

stem: EMI — Psychotherapy defence mechanisms: A 7-year-old girl is angry with her mother for not buying her a toy. In the playground, she shoves another child for no apparent reason. Which defence mechanism is this?
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Displacement is a defence mechanism in which an emotional impulse (particularly aggression) is redirected from a threatening or forbidden target (e.g., mother) to a safer, less threatening target (e.g., another child, a pet, an object). It is considered a 'neurotic' defence — more mature than primitive defences (projection, denial, splitting) but less mature than mature defences (sublimation, humour, altruism). Reference: Vaillant GE. Ego Mechanisms of Defense. American Psychiatric Press, 1992.
Projection involves attributing one's own feelings to others, not redirecting them.
Acting out involves direct behavioural expression of an impulse without redirection to a different target.
Sublimation is channeling impulses into constructive activities.
Reaction formation is behaving opposite to a true feeling.
Splitting is all-good/all-bad categorisation.
Regression involves reverting to an earlier developmental stage.
Repression involves unconsciously blocking unacceptable thoughts from awareness.
Identification involves adopting the characteristics of another person.
Undoing involves trying to reverse or make amends for an unacceptable thought or action.
teaching_point: Displacement is a defence mechanism in which an emotional impulse (particularly aggression) is redirected from a threatening or forbidden target (e.g., mother) to a safer, less threatening target (e.g., another child, a pet, an object). It is considered a 'neurotic' defence — more mature than primitive defences (projection, denial, splitting) but less mature than mature defences (sublimation, humour, altruism). Reference: Vaillant GE. Ego Mechanisms of Defense. American Psychiatric Press, 1992.

stem: EMI — Psychotherapy defence mechanisms: A 35-year-old woman with obsessive-compulsive personality disorder finds herself having intrusive sexual thoughts about a colleague. She becomes excessively meticulous about not making any sexual remarks and volunteers for committees on 'appropriate workplace conduct'. Which defence mechanism is most likely being used?
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Reaction formation is a defence mechanism in which unacceptable or anxiety-provoking impulses are mastered by exaggerated adoption of the opposite stance or behaviour. It is a classic obsessive-compulsive defence. The unacceptable impulse (sexual thoughts towards a colleague) is transformed into its polar opposite (championing workplace conduct). The person is unaware of the true motive — the behaviour is unconsciously driven. Reference: Freud A. The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence. 1936.
Sublimation would channel the sexual impulse into a genuinely valued creative or social activity, not an opposite-behaviour pattern.
Projection would attribute the sexual thoughts to the colleague instead.
Isolation of affect would separate the idea from the associated feeling, not produce the opposite behaviour.
Undoing involves ritualistic acts to magically reverse a thought or action.
Intellectualisation involves excessive abstract reasoning to avoid emotional experience.
Denial involves refusing to acknowledge the impulse at all.
Rationalisation involves creating logical excuses.
Identification with the aggressor involves adopting the traits of a feared person.
Altruism involves serving others to unconsciously fulfil one's own needs.
teaching_point: Reaction formation is a defence mechanism in which unacceptable or anxiety-provoking impulses are mastered by exaggerated adoption of the opposite stance or behaviour. It is a classic obsessive-compulsive defence. The unacceptable impulse (sexual thoughts towards a colleague) is transformed into its polar opposite (championing workplace conduct). The person is unaware of the true motive — the behaviour is unconsciously driven. Reference: Freud A. The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence. 1936.

stem: EMI — Psychotherapy defence mechanisms: A 29-year-old medical student who has a phobia of blood copes with anatomy dissection by focusing purely on the scientific terminology, anatomical nomenclature, and memorising structures — deliberately avoiding any emotional processing of the work. Which defence mechanism is being used?
distractors_rationale: Intellectualisation involves excessive abstract thinking, but the key defence here is separating the idea (dissection) from the emotion (fear/disgust).

This is the correct answer. Isolation of affect (sometimes called isolation of affect from idea) is a defence mechanism in which an unacceptable or threatening idea is separated from the emotional response it would normally trigger. The idea enters consciousness, but the associated feeling is suppressed unconsciously. It is common in obsessive-compulsive and some phobic individuals. Intellectualisation is closely related and often co-occurs — the person focuses on abstract intellectual aspects to further distance themselves emotionally. Reference: Freud S. (1926). Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety.
Rationalisation would involve finding logical justifications for avoidance, not changing the way the information is processed.
Sublimation would channel the fear into a socially valued activity.
Denial would involve refusing to acknowledge the emotional experience at all.
Suppression is a conscious effort to push away unpleasant thoughts; isolation of affect is unconscious.
Undoing involves ritualistic reparative acts.
Reaction formation would involve exaggerated opposite behaviour.
Dissociation involves a disturbance of consciousness, identity, or memory.
Compartmentalisation is not a classic psychoanalytic defence mechanism.
teaching_point: Isolation of affect (sometimes called isolation of affect from idea) is a defence mechanism in which an unacceptable or threatening idea is separated from the emotional response it would normally trigger. The idea enters consciousness, but the associated feeling is suppressed unconsciously. It is common in obsessive-compulsive and some phobic individuals. Intellectualisation is closely related and often co-occurs — the person focuses on abstract intellectual aspects to further distance themselves emotionally. Reference: Freud S. (1926). Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety.

stem: EMI — Psychological learning theories: A child is learning to clean his room. His mother first praises him for picking up one toy, then for picking up all his toys, and later for making his bed as well. Over time, she only praises him when the entire room is tidy. Which behavioural concept does this illustrate?
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Shaping (also called 'successive approximation') is an operant conditioning technique in which behaviours that are progressively closer to the target behaviour are reinforced. Initially, any behaviour that remotely resembles the target is reinforced. The criteria for reinforcement are gradually raised until only the exact target behaviour is reinforced. It is particularly useful for teaching complex behaviours or working with patients with severe developmental disabilities. Reference: Skinner BF. Science and Human Behavior. 1953.
Premack principle uses high-frequency behaviour to reinforce low-frequency behaviour (e.g., 'finish homework then play'), not successive approximation.
Classical conditioning involves pairing a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus to produce a conditioned response.
Operant conditioning (positive reinforcement) is the broader principle but shaping is the specific technique of reinforcing successive approximations.
Discriminative learning involves responding only to specific stimuli, not progressive approximations.
Extinction involves withholding reinforcement to eliminate a behaviour.
Chaining involves linking a series of behaviours together in sequence.
Generalisation involves responding to similar stimuli as the original conditioned stimulus.
Intermittent reinforcement is when reinforcement is delivered only some of the time.
Negative reinforcement involves removing an aversive stimulus to increase a behaviour.
teaching_point: Shaping (also called 'successive approximation') is an operant conditioning technique in which behaviours that are progressively closer to the target behaviour are reinforced. Initially, any behaviour that remotely resembles the target is reinforced. The criteria for reinforcement are gradually raised until only the exact target behaviour is reinforced. It is particularly useful for teaching complex behaviours or working with patients with severe developmental disabilities. Reference: Skinner BF. Science and Human Behavior. 1953.

stem: EMI — Psychological learning theories: A 6-year-old girl was playing with her neighbour's dog without fear. One day, the dog snapped and bit her hand. She now becomes frightened and cries whenever she sees any dog. Which behavioural concept does this illustrate?
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. This illustrates classical (Pavlovian) conditioning with stimulus generalisation. A previously neutral stimulus (dog — CS) associated with an aversive event (bite — UCS) produces a conditioned fear response (CR). Generalisation occurs when similar stimuli (all dogs) also elicit the fear response. This is the basis for systematic desensitisation and exposure therapy — the phobic patient learns to discriminate that not all dogs are dangerous (stimulus discrimination training). Reference: Pavlov IP. Conditioned Reflexes. 1927.
Acquisition is the initial learning phase, but the specific process here is generalisation to all dogs.
Punishment in operant conditioning refers to a consequence that decreases a behaviour, not the Pavlovian pairing described.
Observational learning involves learning through watching others, not through direct experience.
Stimulus discrimination would be if she only feared that specific dog, not all dogs.
Extinction involves the gradual disappearance of a conditioned response when the CS is presented without the US.
Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated, non-threatening stimulus.
Sensitisation is an increased response to a stimulus over repeated presentations.
Stimulus-specific learning is not a standard behavioural term.
One-trial learning describes how fast the learning occurred, not the process.
teaching_point: This illustrates classical (Pavlovian) conditioning with stimulus generalisation. A previously neutral stimulus (dog — CS) associated with an aversive event (bite — UCS) produces a conditioned fear response (CR). Generalisation occurs when similar stimuli (all dogs) also elicit the fear response. stem: EMI — Substance misuse intoxication syndromes: A 22-year-old woman presents with pinpoint pupils, clammy skin, respiratory depression (respiratory rate 8/min), and reduced level of consciousness. stem: EMI — Learning Disability syndromes: A 12-year-old boy is referred with intellectual disability (moderate), a long narrow face, prominent large ears, and macro-orchidism. He has a history of hyperactivity, anxiety, and avoids eye contact. He has a family history of intellectual disability on his mother's side. Which syndrome is most likely?
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability (CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene at Xq27.3). Key physical features: long narrow face, large protruding ears, prominent jaw, macro-orchidism (post-pubertal). Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) presents with upslanting palpebral fissures, flat facial profile, single palmar crease, and intellectual disability — not large ears, long face, or macro-orchidism.
Williams syndrome involves elfin facies, cardiovascular disease (supravalvular aortic stenosis), and a friendly social phenotype — not macro-orchidism.
Prader-Willi syndrome features neonatal hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, and small hands/feet — not the dysmorphic features described.
Angelman syndrome (maternal 15q11-13 deletion) features microcephaly, ataxic gait, hand-flapping, and a happy demeanour — not large ears or macro-orchidism.
22q11.2 deletion syndrome involves cleft palate, cardiac abnormalities, and conotruncal heart defects — not macro-orchidism.
Tuberous sclerosis features hamartomas, seizures, and ash-leaf macules — not this dysmorphic picture.
Rett syndrome affects girls, with regression after 6-18 months, microcephaly, and hand-wringing.
Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) presents in adolescence with tall stature, hypogonadism, and gynaecomastia — not typically ID in childhood.
Turner syndrome (XO) features short stature, webbed neck, and gonadal dysgenesis in females.

stem: SBA — A 52-year-old forensic psychiatrist is appointed as an expert witness in a criminal case. The defendant is charged with murder and has a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia with active psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations commanding him to 'defend himself') at the time of the offence. The psychiatrist is asked to provide an opinion on whether the defendant knew that his actions were wrong at the time of the offence. Which legal test is being applied here, and what is the MOST likely outcome of such an assessment?
options: The M'Naghten Rules — the defendant is likely to be found not guilty by reason of insanity if the delusions directly caused him to believe he was acting in self-defence
The M'Naghten Rules — the defendant is likely to be found fit to plead and convicted
Diminished responsibility — the defendant is likely to receive a hospital order with restrictions
Diminished responsibility — the defendant is likely to be convicted of manslaughter rather than murder
Unfitness to plead — the defendant is likely to be found unfit and receive a hospital disposal
Automatism — the defendant is likely to be acquitted
Involuntary intoxication — the defendant is likely to receive a hospital disposal
The principle of doli incapax — the defendant is too unwell to be held criminally responsible
Corpus delicti — the defendant cannot be found guilty if there is insufficient evidence
Habeas corpus — the defendant's detention is unlawful as there has been no preliminary hearing
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. The M'Naghten Rules (1843) provide the legal test for insanity in criminal law: (1) at the time of the offence, the defendant must have been suffering from a defect of reason from disease of the mind, and (2) as a result, he either did not know the nature and quality of his act, OR he did not know it was wrong. Under English law, a person found not guilty by reason of insanity receives a disposal ranging from a hospital order (with/without restrictions) to an absolute discharge — the court has discretion since the 1991 amendment. The use of the M'Naghten Rules in England and Wales has declined significantly since diminished responsibility was introduced (Homicide Act 1957) — insanity is rarely pleaded because it carries a potentially indeterminate disposal. Reference: Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991; Homicide Act 1957.

stem: SBA — A 34-year-old man is referred by the probation service for a forensic psychiatry assessment after being convicted of stalking his ex-girlfriend following their separation 6 months ago. He calls her repeatedly, leaves notes on her car, waits outside her workplace, and has sent her multiple messages expressing his enduring love and his belief that they are 'destined to be together'. He cannot accept that the relationship has ended and continues to hope for reconciliation. Which typology of stalking does he most closely fit according to the Mullen et al. classification?
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Mullen et al. (1999, 2000) classified five stalking typologies: (1) Rejected stalker — pursues ex-intimate, motivated by reconciliation or revenge, (2) Intimacy seeker — seeks a relationship with someone they believe loves them (often delusional), (3) Incompetent suitor — lacks social skills, seeks a brief relationship, (4) Resentful stalker — motivated by grievance and vengeance, (5) Predatory stalker — gathers information as prelude to sexual assault. The intimacy seeker believes the target loves them (may have erotomanic delusions); the rejected stalker cannot accept the relationship has ended but knows it existed. Reference: Mullen PE et al. Stalking: A review and classification. Aust N Z J Psychiatry 1999;33(6):835-43.
The rejected stalker pursues an ex-intimate to achieve reconciliation OR to exact revenge — this man is not seeking vengeance but reconciliation.
The resentful stalker pursues victims to exact revenge for a perceived injury or grievance — not the case here.
The incompetent suitor pursues a stranger or acquaintance for a brief sexual encounter or date, not a former partner.
The predatory stalker targets strangers for sexual gratification, often as a prelude to sexual assault.
Erotomanic stalker has a delusional belief that the target loves them — this man knows the relationship existed but cannot accept it has ended.
Vengeance stalker is a subtype of resentful stalker with a specific grudge.
Domestic violence stalker is not a Mullen typology category.
Celebrity stalker refers to stalking a public figure.
Cyberstalker refers to the medium used, not the motivation.

stem: SBA — A 72-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer's disease (MMSE 17/30) is an inpatient on a general medical ward awaiting discharge to a residential care home. She cannot reliably recall the risks and benefits of the proposed placement. The family is requesting a Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) authorisation. Her son, with whom she has a close relationship, has Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) for Health and Welfare. Which of the following statements BEST describes the legal position regarding the DoLS application?
options: DoLS authorisation is not required if the son, as LPA holder, consents to the placement

If the patient objects to the placement, a DoLS authorisation cannot be granted
The son can consent to the care home placement under his LPA, making DoLS unnecessary
The requirement for DoLS applies only to care homes and not to hospitals
An Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA) must be appointed in all cases where DoLS is considered
The patient's GP can grant the DoLS authorisation as an urgent application
The MHA 1983 has no application to people with dementia who lack capacity
distractors_rationale: LPA for Health and Welfare does not give the attorney the power to consent to a deprivation of liberty — only the Court of Protection can authorise a deprivation of liberty (Supreme Court decision in Cheshire West 2014).
DoLS authorisation is for hospitals and care homes and the 'acid test' (Cheshire West) applies regardless of LPAs.

The MHA 1983 can be used if the person needs treatment for a mental disorder and refuses or requires detention, but DoLS is the appropriate framework for people who lack capacity to decide on residence/care and do not meet MHA criteria.
Court of Protection approval is not required for every care home placement — DoLS provides the framework for cases where the placement amounts to a deprivation of liberty.
Objection does not preclude DoLS — it triggers an assessment of whether DoLS is appropriate.

teaching_point: DoLS (Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards) were introduced under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA 2005) via the Mental Health Act 2007 amendments. If these conditions are met, DoLS authorisation is required regardless of LPA, family consent, or the person's cooperation. stem: SBA — A 28-year-old woman with a 3-year history of anorexia nervosa (restrictive type, current BMI 13.8 kg/m²) is being treated on a medical ward for severe bradycardia (38 bpm) and electrolyte disturbances. options: The MHA 1983 is the appropriate framework because feeding can be considered treatment for the mental disorder (anorexia nervosa) under Section 145 MHA, and the MCA 2005 cannot be used if the patient meets MHA criteria
The MCA 2005 is sufficient — feeding can be provided as life-sustaining treatment in the patient's best interests under Section 4 MCA, and the MHA is not required
The MCA 2005 cannot be used to authorise force-feeding as it would amount to a deprivation of liberty — only the MHA can provide this authority
Nasogastric feeding is a medical treatment requiring the patient's consent and cannot be given against her will under any legal framework
The Court of Protection must be asked to authorise the feeding as it involves a serious interference with Article 8 rights
Under the MCA 2005, an LPA for Health and Welfare or a court-appointed deputy can consent to nasogastric feeding even if the patient refuses
The force-feeding of a patient with anorexia is a criminal act of battery regardless of the legal framework used
The patient should be transferred to a specialist eating disorders unit — no legal framework is needed as this is a clinical decision
Section 5 MHA (emergency holding power) can be used by the nurse to begin nasogastric feeding immediately
The patient's refusal is valid as she retains capacity — anorexia nervosa does not automatically impair capacity regarding feeding decisions
distractors_rationale: This is the correct answer. Nasogastric feeding of a patient with severe anorexia nervosa can be lawful under the MHA 1983 as treatment for the mental disorder. Section 145 MHA defines medical treatment as including 'nursing, care, habilitation and rehabilitation under medical supervision'. The Court of Appeal in Re KB (Adult) (Mental Patient: Medical Treatment) [1994] confirmed that feeding a patient with anorexia against her will can be treatment for the mental disorder. In practice, a combination of MHA + MCA + Court of Protection may be used depending on the specific circumstances. The key principle: the MHA takes precedence over the MCA when the person needs treatment for a mental disorder AND meets MHA criteria for detention. Reference: MHA 1983 s.145; MCA 2005 s.29; Re KB [1994]; R v Collins and Ashworth Hospital [1998] — also confirming nasogastric feeding under MHA is lawful.

LPA/Deputy cannot consent to treatment that the patient physically resists — this would require detention.
Case law (R v Collins, Re W) has confirmed that nasogastric feeding under the MHA is lawful and not battery.
Transfer to a specialist unit does not resolve the legal authority needed to feed against the patient's will.
Section 5 MHA is a holding power for nurses (Section 5(4)) or doctors (Section 5(2)) — it cannot authorise forcible feeding as a treatment.
